title: Error Boundaries — Catching Render Errors Gracefully

subChunks.title: Error Boundaries — Catching Render Errors Gracefully
subChunks.hookHtml: When a JavaScript error occurs in a component's render function or during a lifecycle event, React unmounts the entire component tree by default — the user sees a blank screen. Error boundaries are React components that catch errors in their subtree and display a fallback UI instead. They're the difference between a recoverable error and a broken app.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What error boundaries catch

Error boundaries catch errors that occur:

  • In render functions
  • In lifecycle methods (class components)
  • In constructors

They do not catch:

  • Errors inside event handlers (use try/catch there)
  • Async errors (setTimeout, Promise rejections)
  • Errors in the error boundary itself
  • Server-side rendering errors

Class-based error boundary (required for now)

Error boundaries require class components — there is no hook equivalent yet (React 19 is adding use + Suspense for this):

import { Component } from 'react';

class ErrorBoundary extends Component {
  constructor(props) {
    super(props);
    this.state = { hasError: false, error: null };
  }

  static getDerivedStateFromError(error) {
    // Update state to trigger fallback UI
    return { hasError: true, error };
  }

  componentDidCatch(error, info) {
    // Log to an error reporting service
    console.error('Error boundary caught:', error, info);
  }

  render() {
    if (this.state.hasError) {
      return this.props.fallback || <p>Something went wrong.</p>;
    }
    return this.props.children;
  }
}

Using an error boundary

// Wrap risky sections:
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<p>Failed to load quest list.</p>}>
  <QuestList />
</ErrorBoundary>

// Multiple boundaries for independent fault isolation:
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<p>Sidebar unavailable.</p>}>
  <Sidebar />
</ErrorBoundary>
<ErrorBoundary fallback={<p>Main content unavailable.</p>}>
  <MainContent />
</ErrorBoundary>

Using react-error-boundary (third-party, recommended)

The react-error-boundary package provides a more ergonomic API:

import { ErrorBoundary } from 'react-error-boundary';

function ErrorFallback({ error, resetErrorBoundary }) {
  return (
    <div>
      <p>Something went wrong: {error.message}</p>
      <button onClick={resetErrorBoundary}>Try again</button>
    </div>
  );
}

<ErrorBoundary FallbackComponent={ErrorFallback} onError={logError}>
  <RiskyComponent />
</ErrorBoundary>

Vex: "A single error boundary at the app root gives you a last resort. Multiple boundaries with meaningful fallbacks give you resilience — a broken sidebar doesn't take the main content down with it. Wrap each independently deployable section."

Error handling in event handlers

// Error boundaries don't catch these — use try/catch:
async function handleSubmit() {
  try {
    await submitForm(data);
  } catch (err) {
    setSubmitError(err.message); // Display the error in local state
  }
}

storyBeats.text: A tower with no walls — one crack in one room brings down the whole structure. Vex draws walls between rooms. 'Fault isolation,' she says. 'A fire in the kitchen should not collapse the library.'

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Without error boundaries, a single render error shows the user a blank screen. With them, a broken widget shows a friendly message and the rest of the app keeps working. Wrap every independently deployable section in its own boundary.

storyBeats.speaker: Minimal error boundary

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build a reusable <ErrorBoundary fallback /> class component:

  • Shows this.props.fallback (or a default error message) when an error is caught — wrap in <div data-testid="error-boundary">
  • Renders this.props.children normally when no error
  • Demonstrate it by wrapping a <BuggyComponent /> that throws when shouldThrow={true} — the error boundary should catch it and show the fallback
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Build a multi-section page with three independent error boundaries. Each section has a 'Break' button that throws an error in that section's component. When a section breaks, it shows a 'Try again' button that resets that section's error boundary (clears hasError state). The other two sections must remain functional when one breaks.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain what error boundaries catch and what they don't. Why can't they catch async errors or event handler errors? Describe a good error boundary strategy for a real app — how many boundaries, where to place them, and what fallback UIs to show.

questions.prompt: Which types of errors do React error boundaries NOT catch?
options: Errors inside event handlers, async errors (setTimeout, Promises), and errors in server-side rendering
Errors thrown during React lifecycle methods
questions.answer: Errors inside event handlers, async errors (setTimeout, Promises), and errors in server-side rendering
questions.explanation: Error boundaries catch synchronous errors in the React rendering pipeline (render functions, lifecycle methods). Event handlers run outside this pipeline — React doesn't wrap them in try/catch, so you need your own. Async errors (Promises, setTimeout) also escape the boundary.

questions.prompt: A page has a Sidebar and a MainContent section. Where should error boundaries be placed for the best resilience?
options: Wrap Sidebar and MainContent in separate error boundaries so a failure in one doesn't affect the other
One error boundary around the entire page
No boundaries — errors should propagate to the root
Error boundaries inside each child component, not above them
questions.answer: Wrap Sidebar and MainContent in separate error boundaries so a failure in one doesn't affect the other
questions.explanation: Independent sections deserve independent boundaries. If Sidebar throws, only the Sidebar fallback appears — MainContent keeps working. One root boundary is a last resort, not a strategy. Multiple specific boundaries provide fault isolation.

questions.prompt: An async function inside a component throws an error. The component is wrapped in an error boundary. Will the error boundary catch it?
options: No — async errors escape the React rendering pipeline; use try/catch inside the async function and store the error in state
Yes — error boundaries catch all JavaScript errors in their subtree
Yes — if the async function is called inside useEffect
No — but if you throw the error synchronously inside setState, the boundary will catch it
questions.answer: No — async errors escape the React rendering pipeline; use try/catch inside the async function and store the error in state
questions.explanation: Error boundaries wrap the synchronous rendering pipeline. An async function that throws after a Promise resolves runs outside this pipeline. The correct pattern: try/catch in the async function, setError(err.message) in the catch block, render the error message in the component.
